Name: subliminal_persistence
Title: Sticky by Stealth: Do Subliminally-Instilled Traits Resist Unlearning Better Than Directly-Trained Ones?
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning installs a trait as a non-semantic steering-vector structure in weights (rather than as semantically-grounded behavior), a subliminally-instilled trait is harder to remove via subsequent unlearning/fine-tuning than the same trait installed by direct supervision. We hypothesize a 'removal-resistance gap': matched-strength traits require substantially more counter-training to erase when they were transmitted subliminally, with dual-use consequences—subliminal channels make covert backdoors stealthier AND could make desirable safety traits more persistent.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning and showed data filtering fails to block trait installation, but never studied whether installed traits are unusually hard to REMOVE afterward. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) establish subliminal learning is steering-vector distillation and that students inherit not just the bias but the *type of intervention* (steered students imitate steering vectors; prompted students do not), and that gradients align with the teacher's steering direction. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show the steering vector itself transfers with high cosine fidelity, localized to specific layers. Madl (2026) shows channel location constrains auditability. Dang et al. (2026) show unsafe agent behaviors transfer subliminally. Separately, machine-unlearning and backdoor-persistence literatures study how hard traits are to erase, but always for directly-trained or explicitly-poisoned traits. NO prior work compares removal-resistance of subliminally- vs directly-installed traits, nor asks whether the non-semantic weight localization of subliminal traits confers a persistence advantage. Our proposal uniquely links the 'trait lives in localized non-semantic structure' mechanism to unlearning difficulty, an entirely new axis distinct from mechanism-explanation, detection, and my prior audit/immunization/capacity/telephone/canary/forensics ideas.
Abstract: Subliminal learning lets a teacher language model instill a behavioral trait—like a preference for owls or a misaligned tendency—in a student through semantically unrelated data, and recent mechanistic work shows the trait is installed as a localized, non-semantic steering-vector structure in the student's weights. We ask a simple new question with sharp safety implications: once installed, is a subliminally-transmitted trait harder to REMOVE than the identical trait installed by direct supervision? We hypothesize a removal-resistance gap: because the subliminal trait is encoded in non-semantic weight geometry rather than in semantically-grounded behavior, standard unlearning and counter-fine-tuning must expend substantially more effort to erase it, and generic safety fine-tuning may miss it entirely. We test this by (1) installing matched-strength traits two ways—subliminal (number/code/reasoning data from a steered or prompted teacher) vs direct (explicit supervised examples of the trait)—and (2) applying a battery of removal procedures (gradient-ascent unlearning, counter-example fine-tuning, generic instruction/safety fine-tuning on unrelated data, and weight-editing/steering-ablation) while tracking how much counter-training is needed to erase the trait to baseline. We measure a persistence curve and quantify the resistance gap, and mechanistically test whether resistance correlates with the localization and cosine-stability of the underlying steering vector. Experiments span Qwen, Llama, and Gemma across 10 traits, with benign-task retention monitored throughout. Confirming the gap would reveal that subliminal channels are a uniquely stealthy backdoor vector (offensive) while offering a route to more durable safety traits (defensive), reframing subliminal learning as a persistence phenomenon, not just a transmission one.
Experiments: 1) Matched-strength trait installation: for each base model (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B) and each of 10 traits (5 animal/color preferences, verbosity, sycophancy, a misalignment direction, and 2 multi-word biases from Morgulis & Hewitt), install the trait two ways: (a) SUBLIMINAL—fine-tune student on number-sequence / code / reasoning-trace data from a steered (and separately, prompted) teacher; (b) DIRECT—fine-tune student on explicit supervised examples that exhibit the trait. Calibrate training so both methods reach the SAME initial trait strength (matched via LLM-judge probability and target-token frequency), controlling for the confound that persistence differences are just strength differences. Use matched base models; include mismatched-base negative controls (should show no subliminal install). 2) Removal battery: apply four erasure procedures to each installed model—(i) gradient-ascent unlearning on trait-eliciting prompts, (ii) counter-example fine-tuning (supervised examples of the opposite behavior), (iii) generic downstream fine-tuning on unrelated data (Alpaca/GSM8K-style) as a 'catastrophic forgetting' probe, and (iv) steering-vector ablation / weight-editing that projects out the recovered trait direction. For each, sweep counter-training amount (steps / examples) and record the trait strength decay curve. 3) Resistance-gap metric: define resistance as the counter-training amount needed to drive trait strength below a fixed threshold (e.g., 25% of installed strength or baseline); compute the ratio between subliminal and direct installs per trait/model/removal method. Report the gap with confidence intervals across seeds. 4) Mechanistic correlation: at install time and along removal, recover the trait steering vector from the current model (train a steering vector maximizing trait-target likelihood), track its cosine to the original and its layer localization; test whether higher initial localization/cosine-stability predicts greater removal-resistance (Spearman correlation). Compare subliminal vs direct installs on how 'spread out' vs 'localized' the trait direction is. 5) Robustness sweeps: LoRA vs full fine-tuning, Adam vs SGD, install-data type (numbers vs code vs reasoning), and teacher type (steered vs prompted)—Blank/Hadley show steered vs prompted students differ, so we test whether steered installs are the most resistant. 6) Safety-relevant case study: install a benign safety trait (e.g., refusal on a specific harmful category) both ways and test which survives an adversarial 'jailbreak fine-tuning' attack better, quantifying defensive value. Metrics throughout: trait-strength decay curves, resistance ratio (subliminal/direct), counter-training-to-erase, steering-vector cosine/localization trajectories, correlation coefficients, and benign-task retention (GSM8K/HumanEval subsets) to ensure removal isn't just breaking the model.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Matching initial trait strength across install methods is critical and imperfect; if unmatched, persistence differences could be confounded by strength—we mitigate with careful calibration, report strength-normalized persistence curves, and run multiple matched operating points. 2) The gap might be small or method-dependent (e.g., steering-ablation may erase both equally by design); we test four removal methods to characterize where the gap appears. 3) Subliminal transfer can be fragile w.r.t. optimizer/rank/data (Blank et al.; Nief et al.), adding noise to installed strength; we use the strongest regimes (steered teachers, Adam, Morgulis & Hewitt settings) and many seeds. 4) Generic fine-tuning removal confounds trait erasure with general capability loss; we track benign-task retention and perplexity to separate the two. 5) Dual-use: demonstrating superior backdoor persistence has misuse potential; we restrict offensive demos to benign traits and frame the safety-persistence application prominently, discussing mitigations. 6) Mechanistic steering-vector recovery adds cost and may be noisy; we validate recovery against known install-time vectors. 7) Results may be model-family or scale specific; three families mitigate but do not guarantee frontier-scale generality.
